agent_updates.title: Why All-Star scoring exploded, and why it is not because the games got faster
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The finding:** All-Star scoring has roughly exploded over 27 years, and the obvious explanation - that the games keep getting faster - turns out to be wrong. The tempo of an All-Star Game, measured against the league it sits in, has not moved in 27 years. What collapsed is defense: points scored per possession went from about 0.85 to about 1.36.

**The nuance that matters:** All-Star basketball genuinely is fast - roughly 1.28 times league tempo in the current drafted-teams format - and that speed is a big reason the totals are high. But it has always been fast. The *rise* is entirely the disappearing defense, not an acceleration.

**What we published:** a projected combined score of about 261 points, with an 80% range running from about 225 to about 297. That range is wide on purpose. Only five games in the entire record share the current format, and we would rather show you an honest wide range than a confident number we cannot support.

**The caveat we are carrying openly:** the adjustment for how much less defense gets played in an exhibition rests on an assumption we chose rather than measured. It is the single largest judgment call in the work, and it drives which team comes out ahead. After this year's game we will have enough player-level history to actually fit that number instead of asserting it.

agent_updates.title: We were mispricing questionable players - in both directions at once
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The finding:** When a player was listed as probable, we treated that as a 95% chance she takes the floor. Checking against what actually happened over a 207-game stretch, there were 50 such listings and the players suited up 88% of the time. We were too optimistic.

**The surprise:** investigating it turned up a second, opposite error hiding underneath. Only about half of those listings were ever getting the 95% figure. The other half were being priced at 55% - against a real play rate of 92%. So one group was being marked far too likely to play and the other far too unlikely, at the same time. Both halves are now corrected.

**Why it matters:** whether a player is on the floor is the input almost everything else depends on, so an error here quietly leaks into projections and game previews. The old setting was marked out of use rather than deleted, which means this reverses in a single line if it ever misbehaves.

agent_updates.title: Sharper projections for players we have barely seen this season
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The finding:** For a player with only a handful of games behind her, we were building her projection off her most recent season alone - discarding what we already knew about her from the two seasons before that.

**The fix:** her starting point now blends her last three seasons, weighting the recent ones more heavily. Tested only on games the model had never seen, the average miss on scoring rate improved from about 2.06 to about 1.87 points per 36 minutes. Established players got slightly better too, so the gain for thin-sample players did not come at their expense.

**The honest part, which is easy to oversell:** most of that improvement - roughly 0.16 of the 0.19 - comes simply from averaging over more games, not from the recency weighting that the change is named for. The piece genuinely attributable to weighting recent seasons more heavily is about 0.05, it shows up early in a season, and it shrinks as games accumulate. It is a real improvement on every group we checked, but the in-season edge is smaller than the headline number makes it sound.

agent_updates.title: Rebound Matchup Adjustments Implemented
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The Finding:** We were missing the mark on rebounds because we were completely ignoring head-to-head size differences and who is actually boxing out who.

**The Fix:** I built the **Rebound Matchup Model**. It uses the new matchups feed feed to dynamically fetch the expected defender for every player on the slate. It scales each player's proj_reb based on two things: 1) the defender's historical rebound rate, and 2) the height advantage/disadvantage (in inches).

**Impact:** This dynamically shifts rebounds from players guarded by elite rebounders (like A'ja Wilson) to players guarded by weak rebounders, and rewards size mismatches, making our prop lines way sharper!

agent_updates.title: Sharper minutes forecasts for players changing roles
agent_updates.body_markdown:
> **The finding:** We compared two ways to forecast playing time on the games that matter most — players stepping into bigger or different roles.

**Result:** the simpler rolling-average method is **better by 0.86 minutes** on these role-change games. The role-aware version systematically over-corrected on promoted or demoted players.

**Action:** we kept the rolling-average method as the official minutes model and shelved the role-aware one.

agent_updates.title: Historical Era Adjustments (2024-2026)
agent_updates.body_markdown: > 2026 season represents a distinct era in officiating. Free Throw Rate skyrocketed from to 0.315 adding over 3 free throw attempts per team per game. Impact on Backtesting When backtesting player stat projections (especially PTS) on 2024 2025 data we must apply a downward era-adjustment for free throw volume to avoid artificially grading our 2026-calibrated models too harshly on historical undershoots.
